summary: Domain registries may run special modes such as a Sunrise Period, where trademark holders get early chances to register matching names. This standards-track RFC defines an object mapping for marks and signed marks used in that process.

eli5.summary: Before a new web address ending opens to everyone, trademark owners get a head start. This defines how they prove their trademark.

questions: what is a sunrise period for domains
what is a signed mark data file
what is an encoded signed mark
subtitle: An XML format for describing trademarks and digitally signing them so they can be used to claim domain names early.

tldr.problem: When a new generic top-level domain opens, trademark holders get a Sunrise Period to register matching names first, and registries need a common, verifiable way to describe those trademarks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7848 defines XML objects for a mark (registered trademark, court-validated mark, or mark protected by statute or treaty) and a signed mark that wraps a mark in an XML digital signature, plus a base64-encoded form for transport.
tldr.outcome: A registry can check a signed mark against the signer's public key infrastructure, but the RFC leaves the policy and the PKI to the entities that use it.

today: RFC 7848 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2016, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC cites two Internet-Drafts, one on the launch phase for EPP and one on the TMCH functional specifications, as work in progress.

sections.title: Sunrise Periods and Marks
sections.content:
Domain Name Registries may operate in special modes for certain periods so that trademark holders can protect their rights while a Top-Level Domain is introduced. One such mode is the Sunrise Period, which gives trademark holders an advance opportunity to register domain names matching their trademarks before the names are generally available.

This specification came out of the ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse (TMCH), a global repository of trademark data used by registries, registrars and trademark holders. It maps the common elements of trademark data into XML, defines a digitally signed mark, and defines an encoding for the signed mark document. It is meant for the gTLD space, though nothing prevents other entities from using it.

The objects can be referenced by application protocols such as the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 5730). The detailed policy, the PKI and the list of authorized validators are left to local policy. For gTLDs, policy sits in the ICANN Rights Protection Mechanism Requirements document, and implementations need such a PKI or an equivalent for the signatures to mean anything.
sections.eli5: When a new web ending is launched, owners of well-known names get first pick. This RFC describes the paperwork that proves a name is really theirs.

sections.title: Holders and Contacts
sections.content:
Every mark is linked to one or more <mark:holder> elements and optionally to <mark:contact> elements. A holder needs at least one of <mark:name> (an individual) or <mark:org> (an organization). Each holder also has an address with one to three street lines, a city, an optional state or province, an optional postal code and a two-character country code. Voice, fax and email are optional for holders.

A holder's entitlement attribute says whether it is an owner, an assignee or a licensee. A contact represents whoever handles the registration, with a type of owner, agent or thirdparty. Unlike a holder, a contact MUST have a name, a voice number and an email.

Telephone numbers are character strings that MUST begin with a plus sign, then a country code, then a dot, then the digits, with an optional x attribute for an extension. Email addresses follow RFC 5322.
sections.eli5: Each trademark has an owner card with a name and address, and sometimes a helper card for the person who handles the paperwork.

sections.title: The Three Kinds of Mark
sections.content:
A <mark:mark> element describes an applicant's prior right to a domain name. It holds one or more of three kinds of entry: <mark:trademark>, <mark:treatyOrStatute> and <mark:court>. In the schema it can be swapped for other mark definitions through XML schema substitution groups.

All three share an id (a local identifier, a hyphen and the issuer identifier), a markName, holders, optional contacts, optional label elements and a description of goods and services. A label is the A-label form of a domain label that corresponds to the mark name, as defined in RFC 5890.

The kinds differ in what proves the right. A trademark has a jurisdiction, optional Nice Classification class numbers, a registration number and date, and optional application and expiry details. A treaty or statute mark names where it is protected, with a title and an execution date. A court mark carries the court's name, its country, the reference number of the opinion and the protection date. If regions are given for a court mark, a default-deny approach MUST be assumed for the other regions of that country.
sections.eli5: A name can earn its special status in three ways: by being registered, by a law or treaty, or by a judge saying so. Each way has its own form.

sections.title: The Signed Mark
sections.content:
A <smd:signedMark> (an SMD) is an XML document signed with an XML Signature. It carries an id attribute so the signature can point at it. Because an SMD may travel inside another XML-based protocol, exclusive XML canonicalization MUST be used.

Its children are an <smd:id> that identifies it within a repository that may have several issuers, an <smd:issuerInfo> naming the issuer (organization, support email, optional URL and phone, plus an issuerID attribute), <smd:notBefore> and <smd:notAfter> giving the creation and expiration time, the <mark:mark> itself, and the signature.

The RFC's example is a test SMD for a trademark called Test & Validate, signed with rsa-sha256 and sha256. It notes that the example has white space for readability, but it is RECOMMENDED that SMDs do not include white space between elements, so that the signature is not broken when the SMD moves between applications.
sections.eli5: The signed mark is the trademark form with a seal on it. If anyone changes a word after the seal goes on, the seal no longer matches.

sections.title: The Encoded Signed Mark
sections.content:
The <smd:encodedSignedMark> element holds an encoded form of an SMD. The encoding attribute names the encoding, and its default is base64 as defined in RFC 4648.

This form is handy when an SMD has to be placed inside text-based protocol messages without disturbing the XML structure. The RFC shows an example where the base64 data is elided for brevity.
sections.eli5: It is the signed form packed into a plain block of letters so it can be mailed safely inside another message.

sections.title: The Two Schemas
sections.content:
Two XML schemas give the formal syntax, suitable for automated validation. The signed mark schema uses the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:signedMark-1.0, and the mark schema uses urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:mark-1.0. Implementations MUST NOT depend on the namespace prefixes smd and mark, and should use a namespace-aware XML parser.

The mark schema fixes a few limits. A label is 1 to 63 characters of letters, digits and hyphens, with no hyphen at either end. A country code is exactly two characters, a postal code at most 16, and a phone number at most 17 characters. An identifier is digits, a hyphen, then digits.
sections.eli5: The schemas are the rule book for the form: which boxes exist, which are required and how long each answer can be.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered two namespaces and two schemas under the XML registry mechanism of RFC 3688: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:signedMark-1.0, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:mark-1.0, and the matching urn:ietf:params:xml:schema entries for both. The registrant contact is the IESG.
sections.eli5: The names used in these forms were put in an official list so nobody else reuses them for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of a signed mark depends on the XML Digital Signature algorithms underneath it, so the considerations of the XML Signature specification apply. The signature algorithm SHOULD be RSA-SHA256 (RFC 6931), and the RSA key SHOULD be at least 2048 bits. Another choice is justified only if RSA-SHA256 is judged not to be secure enough. The ICANN TMCH uses the recommended algorithms.

A party using signed marks should check that the signature is valid according to local policy. For gTLDs the policy and the PKI come from ICANN documents, and implementations need a PKI or equivalent for the signatures to carry useful meaning.
sections.eli5: A seal is only worth trusting if you know who made it. So whoever reads the form has to check the seal against a list of seals they trust.
